entities.name: Forma Urbis Romae
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Forma Urbis Romae, also known as the Severan Marble Plan, stands as a monumental testament to the urban planning and architectural prowess of ancient Rome, crafted during the reign of Emperor Septimius Severus between AD 203 and 211. This colossal marble map, measuring approximately 18 by 13 meters, depicted the city of Rome in remarkable detail, showcasing buildings, streets, and other urban features that made it one of the most ambitious cartographic projects of its time. Its creation was largely motivated by the need to document property holdings and urban development, reflecting the complexities of Roman society and governance during a period of considerable change.

The map was meticulously designed based on existing property records and served not only as a navigational tool but also as a statement of imperial authority and urban identity. It was carved into 150 marble slabs, each intricately detailed, providing a visual representation of the city’s layout that has informed historians about Roman architecture and urbanism. Historical sources suggest that the project was executed under the supervision of the architect and surveyor, possibly named Marcellus, highlighting the collaborative efforts necessary for such an extensive undertaking.

In the centuries that followed its creation, the Forma Urbis Romae continued to influence urban planning and cartography, serving as an essential resource for future architects and historians. The remnants of the map, rediscovered in the 16th century, have offered invaluable insights into the urban landscape of ancient Rome, impacting studies in archaeology and history. Its legacy persists in modern mapping practices, underscoring the importance of accurate representation of urban spaces.
